h1:
Koh Chang Viewpoints
Kai Bae, Spots Around the Island, and Sunset Angles
intro: Koh Chang runs long from north to south, with mountains down its middle and a coastal road that climbs and dips the whole way. Every time the road crests a hill, it tends to open up a view of the sea and the little scattered islands. The spot most people know is the Kai Bae Viewpoint, where you get a 180-degree sweep of the sea and 4 islands — but there are plenty of other spots around the island where the sunset is just as good. We'll work through them one by one, telling you which are free, which have a cafe, when the light is best, and what to know about the steep roads before you ride up.

blocks.html: Koh Chang's main beaches and sights are strung along a single road on the west coast — the side that faces the sea and catches the sunset. That's why nearly all the standout viewpoints sit on this side, running from the middle of the island around Klong Prao down past Kai Bae to the southern tip. The east coast is quieter and better suited to sunrise. We'll start with the most famous spot first.

blocks.text: Kai Bae Viewpoint — a 180-degree view of 4 islands

blocks.html: Kai Bae Viewpoint is the most talked-about lookout on Koh Chang. It sits on a hill along the road between Kai Bae Beach and Lonely Beach, and from the top you get a sweep of sea and small islands stretching about 180 degrees in front of you. Four islands stand out clearly: Koh Man Nai, Koh Man Nok, Koh Pli, and Koh Yuak. The blue of the water against the green of the islands makes this a spot people come specifically to photograph and to wait out the sunset.

items: Free entry — there's no charge for the viewpoint, and there's a car park and restrooms.
There's a cafe up top (View Cafe) where you can order coffee or a drink and sit with the view. You just pay normal drink prices, not an entry fee.
The best light is in the evening, about half an hour before sunset when the sky starts to change color.
At low tide you can see sandbars emerge between the islands, which photographs beautifully. Check the tide table ahead of time.

blocks.title: The climb up to Kai Bae is fairly steep
blocks.html: The entrance to Kai Bae Viewpoint is a short, steep slope. If you're riding two-up on a motorbike and aren't used to steep roads, take extra care or park at the bottom and walk up. The evening crowd waiting for sunset fills the car park fast, so give yourself a little extra time and it'll be easier.

blocks.text: Laem Chai Chet — sunset at the end of Klong Prao Beach

blocks.html: Laem Chai Chet sits at the northern end of Klong Prao Beach — a rocky point reaching out into the sea, with boulders and trees leaning into the wind. It's a sunset spot favored by people staying around Klong Prao and White Sand Beach, an easy walk from the road or from the resorts nearby. In the evening the golden light hits the rocks and the water, making for a calmer, quieter photo angle than Kai Bae. If you're staying in this area and don't want to drive far in the evening, this is the convenient choice.

blocks.text: Pha Suk Niran (Laem Sing) — a rocky spot by the sea

blocks.html: Pha Suk Niran is over by Laem Sing, in the north of the island — a flat rock platform by the sea where people stop to shoot the open sea and the big boulders. It's more of a check-in photo spot than a high hilltop lookout, and it suits people staying in the northern zones like White Sand Beach or Laem Sing who want a sea view close by without driving south. The path down over the rocks can be slippery, so shoes with decent grip will keep you safer.

blocks.text: Viewpoints around the island — in driving order

blocks.html: If you drive along the main road on the west coast, you'll hit spots where the road opens up a sea view worth pulling over for. We've put the standout ones in order, with a note on what each is good for.

items.name: Kai Bae Viewpoint
items.blurb: The main one to stop at — a 180-degree view of the sea and 4 islands. Free entry, with a cafe and restrooms. Best at sunset. The climb up is short but steep, so take care if you're riding two-up.
items.meta: Between Kai Bae and Lonely Beach · free entry · cafe

items.name: Laem Chai Chet (Klong Prao)
items.blurb: A rocky point at the end of Klong Prao Beach, an easy walk from accommodation in this area. Lovely sunset, quieter than Kai Bae — good for anyone who doesn't want to drive far in the evening.
items.meta: Northern end of Klong Prao Beach · easy walk

items.name: Pha Suk Niran (Laem Sing)
items.blurb: A rock platform by the sea in the north of the island — a check-in spot with an open sea view and big boulders. Good for people staying around White Sand Beach and Laem Sing. The path down over the rocks is slippery, so watch your footing.
items.meta: Northern zone, Laem Sing · check-in spot

items.name: White Sand Beach (beachside sunset)
items.blurb: A popular beach in the north. In the evening it's an easy place to sit on the sand and watch the sun go down, with beach bars playing music. Good for anyone who wants to watch the sunset with food and drinks on hand.
items.meta: Northern beach · beach bars · easy seating

items.name: Kai Bae Beach (island view off the beach)
items.blurb: Kai Bae Beach itself has a small island just off the sand — at low tide you can walk out to it. It's a sand-level photo angle with the sunset, a different perspective from the viewpoint up the hill.
items.meta: Kai Bae Beach · island off the shore · walkable at low tide

items.name: Bang Bao Fishing Village (lighthouse)
items.blurb: At the end of the west-coast road, a long wooden pier runs out to sea and ends at a white lighthouse — a photo spot with a view of the bay and the fishing boats. The evening light is lovely. It's not a hilltop lookout but a sea-level angle.
items.meta: Southern tip · wooden pier + lighthouse · photos

blocks.title: For sunrise, you'll need to cross to the east coast
blocks.html: Every viewpoint above is on the west coast, facing the sea for the sunset. If you want the sunrise, you'll need to drive across to the east coast around Than Mayom or Salak Phet Bay, which are quiet with few people — but you'll have to get up early and allow time for the drive across the island.

blocks.text: Sea and sunset photo angles — getting the shot right

blocks.html: Koh Chang sits on the eastern side of the Gulf of Thailand, with the sun setting straight into the sea on the west — which means almost every beach on this side gets the full golden light. If you want your photos to come out well, try these tips.

items: Arrive about 30–45 minutes before sunset to claim a spot and wait for the golden-hour light as the sky starts to change. Don't show up right as the sun is dropping, because the good angles are usually taken by then.
Check the tide table for Kai Bae and the various beaches. At low tide you'll see sandbars and rocks emerge, which makes for a nice foreground.
Use a rock, a boat, or a coconut palm as a foreground element to give your sea shots depth so they don't look flat and empty.
Stick around for another 15–20 minutes after sunset (the blue hour), when the sky turns a beautiful blue-purple. Don't rush off.
In the rainy season the sky often closes in — lots of cloud, and you may not see the sun at all. If you're set on shooting the sunset, the clear-sky months of November to April give you better odds.

blocks.text: Getting to the viewpoints + things to watch for

blocks.html: Almost all of Koh Chang's viewpoints are right off the main road on the west coast, easy enough to reach by car or motorbike. But this road is notorious for its steepness and hairpin bends, so come prepared and drive carefully.

items: The road is steep with sharp hairpin bends, especially the stretch from Kai Bae down to Bang Bao. If you're not used to riding a motorbike on steep roads, don't push it — take a red songthaew (shared taxi) or rent a car instead, it's safer.
Take extra care driving back in the dark. After sunset the sky goes dark fast, and the road has few lights. Use your headlights, drive slowly, and keep your distance.
The road is slippery in the rainy season. Leaves and water on the surface make the wheels slip easily, and the climbs up to the viewpoints especially call for caution.
Fill up before heading south. There are few petrol stations on the island and barely any in the south, so check your fuel before heading out to the far viewpoints in the evening.

blocks.text: A one-day viewpoint loop on Koh Chang

items.activity: Start at Pha Suk Niran, Laem Sing, and shoot the rock platform by the sea
items.note: The path down over the rocks is slippery — wear shoes with grip

items.activity: Stop at Laem Chai Chet at the end of Klong Prao Beach and sit in the breeze
items.note: Easy to walk to — a good warm-up before sunset

items.activity: Head up to Kai Bae Viewpoint, claim a spot, and order a drink at the cafe
items.note: Allow extra time — the car park fills fast in the evening

items.activity: Shoot the 4-island view, wait out golden hour into blue hour
items.note: Stay another 15–20 minutes after the sun drops — the sky is beautiful in a different way

items.activity: Drive back to your accommodation or carry on to a beach bar at White Sand Beach
items.note: Driving back in the dark, watch the bends — use your headlights and drive slowly

faq.q: Is Kai Bae Viewpoint free, and what's there?
faq.a: Kai Bae Viewpoint is free — there's no entry charge. There's a car park, restrooms, and a cafe up top where you can sit with the view (you just pay normal drink prices). The draw is the view of the sea and 4 islands — Koh Man Nai, Koh Man Nok, Koh Pli, and Koh Yuak — stretching about 180 degrees.

faq.q: Where's the best sunset on Koh Chang?
faq.a: Kai Bae Viewpoint is the most popular thanks to its wide view of the sea and islands. Next is Laem Chai Chet at the end of Klong Prao Beach, which is quieter and an easy walk. And if you'd rather sit on the sand with food and drinks, White Sand Beach and Kai Bae Beach both have lovely sunsets too.

faq.q: Where can you watch the sunrise on Koh Chang?
faq.a: The famous viewpoints are all on the west coast, which faces the sea for the sunset. For sunrise, you'll need to drive across to the east coast around Than Mayom or Salak Phet Bay, which are quiet with few people — but you'll have to get up early and allow time for the drive across the island.

faq.q: Is it hard to ride a motorbike to Kai Bae Viewpoint?
faq.a: Koh Chang's roads are steep with lots of sharp hairpin bends, especially the stretch from Kai Bae down to Bang Bao, and the climb up to the viewpoint itself is a steep slope. If you're not comfortable riding a motorbike on steep roads, don't push it — take a red songthaew (shared taxi) or rent a car instead, it's safer. Driving back in the dark calls for even more care.

faq.q: When's the best time to photograph the Koh Chang sunset?
faq.a: The clear-sky months of November to April give you the best odds of actually seeing the sun. In the rainy season (May to October) the sky often closes in with lots of cloud. On any given day, arrive about 30–45 minutes before sunset to claim a spot and wait for the golden-hour light, then stick around another 15–20 minutes for the blue hour.
